title: The chain (Avot 1:1)
hookLine: Moses received Torah at Sinai and handed it on: Joshua, elders, prophets, the Great Assembly

cards: In a relay race, nobody runs the whole distance. Each runner carries the baton for one stretch, then reaches out and hands it on. Drop it at the handoff, and the race is over.
The runners don't own the baton. They keep it moving. A book of wisdom could open with its best advice.
This one doesn't. Before a single piece of advice, Pirkei Avot answers a question: where did this come from? Who handed it to whom?

teach.b: Here's Avot's first line, in paraphrase. Moses received Torah from Sinai and handed it to Joshua. Joshua handed it to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and the prophets to the men of the Great Assembly.
That's it. A list of hands. Two Hebrew verbs carry the whole thing.
Kibbel: he received. Masar: he handed over. Kibbel shares its root with kabbalah, which at first simply meant tradition: what's been received.
And masorah, tradition handed down, is usually traced to masar. The rabbis noticed a few things. It says Moses received Torah, without the word the.

Some commentators read that as deliberate: not just the written scroll, but the teaching, the explanations, the way to live it. The oral part, which you can only get from a person. And every link is a person.
The elders who led after him. The prophets, Isaiah, Jeremiah and the rest. And the Great Assembly, which tradition says gathered in Ezra's time, after the exile in Babylon.
By the end of this chapter, the chain runs all the way down to named rabbis, teacher after teacher. That's why Avot begins here.
Everything that follows, be patient, be kind, find a teacher, isn't one clever person's opinion. It arrived through hands. And the day you teach anyone anything, you're a link too.

how: Jewish learning is traditionally passed from teacher to student, and quoting a teaching in the name of the one who said it is a valued practice, which Avot itself praises.

o: the line of kings descended from King David
a list of laws linked together into one long code
teaching passed hand to hand from Moses down the ages

games.q: the first links — tap the pairs.
p: gathered in Ezra's time, tradition says

s: Avot begins with a piece of advice
it begins with the chain: who received Torah and who handed it on.
the word kabbalah comes from the same root as received
kibbel, he received. kabbalah first meant simply tradition.
the first line says Moses received the Torah, with the word the
it says Torah without the; some read that as teaching beyond the written scroll.

games.q: you're opening a book of wisdom for the ages. what goes on the first page?
o: the most important piece of advice.
a list of who handed the teaching to whom.
a warning to take it seriously.
games.why: Avot opens with the chain: Moses to Joshua, to the elders, to the prophets, to the Great Assembly. the advice comes after.

practice: Think back to someone who handed you something that stuck: not always a classroom teacher, maybe a boss, an aunt, an older kid on the bus, a coach who told you the truth.
What did they hand you, and who do you think handed it to them? Hold both of them for a moment, gratefully.

wordCard.voice: The chain. Avot's first line: Moses received Torah at Sinai and handed it on, hand to hand, to Joshua, the elders, the prophets and the Great Assembly.

orig.note: Hebrew: he handed over. The verb of the chain in Avot 1:1.

carryVoice: Your line: handed down. Every link in that chain was somebody's student first. See you tomorrow.
